source.version: arXiv:2409.14634v7 dated 16 May 2026 (arXiv stamp, p. 1); camera-ready text for ACM CAIS '26 with copyright block and DOI 10.1145/3786335.3813161 on p. 1
source.title_on_document: Scideator: Human-LLM Compound System for Scientific Ideation through Facet Recombination and Novelty Evaluation

supplement.where: Appendices A to H inside this PDF (pp. 10-27); no separate online supplement is referenced
supplement.holds: Full user-study design and procedure (A), extended results on remaining CSI factors and self-rated idea qualities (B.1), annotation study (C), extra ablation table (D), sample ideas (E), implementation details (F), UI figures (G), prompt pseudocode (H)

paper_design_summary: Twenty-two computer-science researchers each did two 20-minute research-ideation sessions, one with Scideator (a facet-based LLM ideation system) and one with a baseline tool using the same LLM (gpt-4o) with paper-level free-text prompting, in randomized order and with randomized topics. Outcomes are self-reports: the Creativity Support Index after each session and participants' own 7-point ratings of their two favorite ideas (newness, feasibility, specificity, impact, imaginativeness). Separate model-only ablations evaluate the novelty-checker module against expert labels.

studies.label: Within-subjects user study (Scideator vs same-LLM baseline, research ideation)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two tool conditions (Scideator vs baseline) and which of two preset topics went with each condition
assignment.quote: We conducted a within-subjects study, in which each participant completed tasks for the treatment and baseline conditions in randomized order. The ideation topics for the treatment and baseline conditions were also randomized.
assignment.locator: p. 11, Appendix A.2; also p. 6, Section 4.1

arms.name: Scideator (treatment)
arms.description: Facet-based human-LLM ideation system: retrieves analogous papers, extracts purpose/mechanism/evaluation facets, generates ideas by recombining selected facets; novelty checker in a separate evaluation tab. Some functions disabled for the study (Appendix A.4).

arms.name: Baseline (paper-level interaction)
arms.description: Same LLM (gpt-4o-2024-08-06); participants select input papers and give optional free-text instructions; LLM generates ideas directly; no novelty-checker output.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions stated for the CSI and idea-rating analyses (contributions list N=22). The RQ3 novelty-assessment analysis uses 17 participants: one did not receive the full allotted time and four saw a different novelty-checker version due to an API issue (p. 7, fn. 6). Two participants saved only one idea in a session and were asked to pick a next favorite (p. 12, A.5).
participants.who: Computer-science researchers: 16 PhD students, 5 master's students, 1 industry researcher; 12 HCI and 10 NLP; all had authored at least one paper; paid a $60 Amazon gift card
participants.quote: We recruited 22 computer-science researchers (W: 7, M: 15) through institutional mailing lists and academic social networks. We compensated them with a $60 Amazon gift card.
participants.locator: p. 11, Appendix A.1; p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 3, contributions list (N=22)

ai_tool.name_model: Scideator built on gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (gpt-4o for re-ranking, o3-mini for novelty assessment); baseline uses gpt-4o-2024-08-06
ai_tool.how_used: In both conditions the LLM generates research ideas that the participant selects and saves. Scideator structures the interaction around selectable facets from retrieved analogous papers; the baseline takes input-paper selection plus free-text custom instructions. A novelty-evaluation tab (with Scideator's novelty checker in treatment only, plus a ChatGPT-like chat) followed idea generation.

task.description: Generate and save as many research ideas as possible on an assigned topic (HCI: human-AI collaboration in art, AI tools for education; NLP: LLM hallucinations, LLM explainability) starting from three input papers; then pick two favorite ideas, rate them, and evaluate their novelty
task.duration: 20-minute idea-generation task per condition plus 5-minute novelty evaluation; 105-minute session overall

outcomes.name: Self-rated newness of favorite ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Participants rated their own two favorite ideas on a 7-point scale for how different/new the idea was; no external raters or computed score

contrasts.reported: "rated their favorite ideas' newness on a 7-point scale, showing only a slight advantage for Scideator (median difference: 0.5 points)"; no test statistic or p-value reported

outcomes.name: Self-rated imaginativeness of favorite ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 7-point Likert-type self-rating of each of two favorite ideas; reported as treatment-minus-baseline difference in participants' average ratings

contrasts.reported: imaginativeness (M=0.00, Q1=-0.50, Q3=0.38); no test reported

outcomes.name: Self-rated feasibility, specificity, and impact of favorite ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three 7-point Likert-type self-ratings of each of two favorite ideas; reported as treatment-minus-baseline differences in participants' average ratings

contrasts.reported: feasibility (M=0.00, Q1=-0.50, Q3=0.50), specificity (M=0.00, Q1=-0.88, Q3=0.50); "the baseline tool performed slightly better with respect to generating impactful ideas (M=-0.25, Q1=-0.50, Q3=0.00)"; no tests reported

outcomes.name: Creativity Support Index (CSI)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Validated questionnaire on the tool's creativity support (exploration, expressiveness, enjoyment, immersion, results worth effort), 0-100 scale; rates the experience, not the ideas. Factor-level differences in Figure 5b.

contrasts.reported: CSI scores: Scideator median=70.50 (Q1=57.50, Q3=79.00), baseline median=61.00 (Q1=42.25, Q3=71.50). Wilcoxon signed-rank test, V=208.50, p<.01.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1.1 and footnote 5; p. 13, Figure 5

studies.label: Novelty-checker ablations (retrieval and classifier), model only

participants.who: No human participants; test sets of 58 ideas (retrieval) and 43 held-out ideas (classifier) labeled by the first two authors

ai_tool.how_used: Pipeline variants compared on accuracy of retrieving overlapping papers and classifying idea novelty

task.description: Automated novelty classification of research ideas

company_involvement.description: Co-first author Simra Shahid lists Microsoft (Delhi) as affiliation; Pao Siangliulue, Tom Hope, and Daniel S. Weld list the Allen Institute for AI (a non-profit). Both conditions use OpenAI's gpt-4o; no funding statement found.

eligibility.reason: Within-person design with randomized order of two AI configurations (Scideator vs same-LLM baseline), which satisfies criterion 1 as an ai_design contrast. Only 22 participants (well below 50). All creativity outcomes are self-reports: the Creativity Support Index and participants' own ratings of their favorite ideas; no raters or computed measures score the ideas. The ablations are model-only.

one_line_finding: With 22 CS researchers in a randomized-order within-subjects study, Scideator beat a same-LLM baseline on the self-reported Creativity Support Index (median 70.5 vs 61.0; Wilcoxon V=208.50, p<.01; p. 6, fn. 5), while self-rated newness of favorite ideas differed little (median difference 0.5; p. 6).
open_questions: The paper does not state explicitly that all 22 participants enter the CSI test; the contributions list says N=22 (p. 3) and Figure 5a shows one point per participant.
Whether 'M' in Appendix B.1 is the median or the mean of within-person differences is not stated.
notes: No arm works without AI; the contrast is ai_design. RQ3 (p. 7, Figure 4) compares participants' perceived novelty of their favorite ideas before and after the novelty-evaluation step for 17 participants (sign test on confidence, S=5.00, p=n.s.); this is self-assessment of novelty, not a creativity outcome, so it is not listed as an outcome. The expert annotation study (51 ideas, two authors, Cohen's kappa 0.64 then 0.68; p. 5) built the classifier's in-context examples. Code release is promised 'upon acceptance of the paper' (p. 18, Appendix H); no URL. The markdown renders the specificity Q1 as 0.88; the PDF (p. 12) shows -0.88. Sessions were run with a coordinator and recorded through Google Meet (p. 12, A.5), so coded lab_rct (supervised session).
